body:
Developers who want to try new programming languages or projects flock to GitHub, the Microsoft-owned service for sharing code and gathering communities around open-source software.

Every year, GitHub publishes a "State of the Octoverse" report tracking the most popular languages and projects on the site. Given GitHub's prominence in Silicon Valley and anywhere else code is written, the report is a solid proxy for the larger trends in the industry. [...] While established languages like JavaScript and Java generally dominate the most-popular lists, GitHub also tracks the rising stars: the languages and frameworks whose usage is growing fast.

Stephen O'Grady, a principal analyst and cofounder of RedMonk, said he noticed that these fastest-growing languages have three characteristics.

First, they're versatile. For example, Python can be used for machine learning, data science, and other kinds of data-intensive technical tasks. title: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella on GitHub: 'We are all in on open source'
body:
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella says the company's $7.5 billion purchase of software developer platform GitHub shows, "We are all in on open source."

"Microsoft has heritage here. We were a developer tools company first and now, of course, we are all in on open source, and that's what really brings us together with GitHub," Nadella told CNBC's "Squawk Alley" on Monday. "We're going to operate it as an open platform for any language, any framework, any platform." [...] GitHub's tools have become essential to software developers, who use it to store code, keep track of updates and discuss issues. Nadella said that the "core ethos" of GitHub going forward will remain the same and that Microsoft will run it independently.

Microsoft Vice President Nat Friedman will assume the role of GitHub CEO, Microsoft said. He takes over for the developer platform's founder, Chris Wanstrath, who stepped down 10 months ago.

title: Part 1: The Evolution of AI and AI Chips - and the HBM That Powers Them | Samsung Semiconductor Global
body:
AI GPUs are also evolving with more specialized matrix-compute units and support for multiple numerical precision formats. At the same time, performance optimization is expanding beyond individual chips toward rack-scale architectures that integrate GPUs, CPUs, memory, high-speed interconnects, power delivery, cooling, and software.

To fully utilize accelerator compute resources, data must be available when needed. This is why memory is becoming increasingly important as AI systems evolve. [...] GPUs have traditionally used GDDR to provide high memory bandwidth. Designed for higher per-pin data rates than conventional DDR, GDDR was well suited to early GPU-based AI workloads.

As AI models grew larger, however, systems needed to scale both bandwidth and capacity. Because GDDR devices are placed around the GPU on the board, adding memory requires additional space and routing. Raising per-pin data rates also increases the challenges of power consumption, heat, and signal integrity. [...] AI chips are semiconductors designed or used to efficiently perform AI training and inference. GPUs and AI-specific ASICs are key examples, while CPUs typically handle data preprocessing, workload scheduling, and system management.

GPUs became widely used in AI because their highly parallel architecture, originally developed to process large numbers of pixels simultaneously, is also well suited to the matrix operations at the core of deep learning.

title: Toward a new global AI chip order - Asia Times
body:
The episode may also encourage Chinese regulators to retaliate selectively. But retaliation carries costs. Restricting Nvidia and other US suppliers would raise the price and delay of AI development inside China, even as it strengthens the political case for indigenous alternatives.

#### Europe’s uncomfortable position

Europe is not the central actor in this affair, but it has substantial exposure. [...] Expect tighter end-use and end-user verification, more aggressive enforcement against diversion, and closer scrutiny of buyers in Singapore, Hong Kong, the Middle East and Southeast Asia.

Regulators may focus not only on the chips themselves but on the systems around them: high-bandwidth memory, optical and copper networking, interconnects, servers, cooling infrastructure and access to cloud-based AI capacity. [...] European companies depend on US AI chips, Asian fabrication and packaging, and global data-center infrastructure. At the same time, Europe wants to preserve access to Chinese markets and avoid becoming wholly dependent on American security decisions.

The likely European response will be a compromise: stronger alignment with US controls on re-exports and diversion, alongside renewed investment in sovereign AI and semiconductor capacity.
